§ 3NUTRIENTS

§ 4NUTRITION IN ANIMALS

Nutrients divided into two categories:

  1. 1. Macronutrients: Macronutrients are nutrients that the body needs in large amounts to function, including carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
  2. 2. Micronutrients: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals that the body needs in small amounts for growth, development, and health.

Types of Nutrients:

  • Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Protein, Fats
  • Micronutrients: Vitamins, Minerals

§ 5MACRONUTRIENTS

Carbohydrates

  • Carbohydrates are biomolecules composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, primarily used as a source of energy in living organisms.
  • These are quick form of energy.
  • 4 calories are released from 1 gm of carbohydrates.

Carbohydrates Classification:

  • Carbohydrates → Simple (made up of one or two sugar units), Complex (made up of many sugar units)
  • Simple → Monosaccharides (Simplest form, E.g. Glucose, Fructose (in fruits/honey), Galactose, etc.), Disaccharides (Formed when two monosaccharide units are joined together, E.g. Sucrose, Lactose (milk sugar), Maltose (grain sugar), etc.)
  • Complex → Polysaccharides (Complex carbohydrates that are formed with many sugar units joined together. E.g. Glycogen, Starch, Cellulose, etc.)

Starch: Present in potato.

Fats

  • Fats are a crucial type of nutrient, vital for energy, building cell structures, and supporting various bodily functions.
  • Adipose tissues in our body store fats in the form of triglycerides.

9 calories are released from 1 gm of fat.

Types:

  1. 1. Saturated Fats: They are not easily digested as the molecules are tightly packed together. They have higher melting point and are found in red meat, pork, etc.
  2. 2. Unsaturated Fats: They are easily digested in our body and healthier in comparison to saturated fats. They are found in vegetable oil, nuts, and seeds.

Nuts, vegetable oil, fish are rich source of Omega-3.

Proteins

  • Proteins are built from smaller units called amino acids.
  • Requirement: 0.8 gm/kg of body weight per day.
  • Present in: Egg, yolk, soybeans, pulses, chicken, fish, etc.

Proteins in:

  • Milk: Casein
  • Hair/Nail: Keratin
  • Rice: Glutelin, Albumin
  • Grains: Gluten
  • Egg white: Albumin

The white part of an egg solidifies when cooked due to the process of protein denaturation.

Amino Acids

  • Amino acids are the fundamental building blocks of proteins.
  • There are total 20 amino acids, out of which 9 are essential amino acids.

Types:

  1. 1. Essential Amino Acids: Essential amino acids, which the body cannot synthesize, must be obtained through the diet.
Amino AcidsFunctions
HistidineImportant for growth, tissue repair, and production of histamine (immune response)
IsoleucineHelps in muscle metabolism and energy regulation; found in muscle tissue
LeucineStimulates protein synthesis, muscle repair, and regulates blood sugar levels
LysineAids calcium absorption, collagen formation, and immune system function
MethionineInvolved in metabolism and detoxification; precursor of other amino acids
PhenylalaninePrecursor to neurotransmitters (dopamine, epinephrine); improves mood and alertness
ThreonineHelps with protein balance, tooth enamel, and fat metabolism
TryptophanPrecursor of serotonin and melatonin (affects mood and sleep)
ValinePromotes muscle growth and tissue repair; provides energy
  1. 2. Non-Essential Amino Acids: Non-essential amino acids can be produced by the body, but certain circumstances can make them temporarily essential.
  • → Types: Glycine, Serine, Proline, Glutamic acid, Alanine, Aspartic acid, Cystine, Tyrosine, Asparagine, and Glutamine.

Diseases Caused by Deficiency of Proteins

Kwashiorkor

  • Kwashiorkor is a type of malnutrition characterized by severe protein deficiency. It causes fluid retention and a swollen, distended abdomen.
  • Kwashiorkor most commonly affects children, particularly in developing countries with high levels of poverty and food insecurity.

§ 6NUTRIENTS

Marasmus

  • Marasmus is a severe form of malnutrition caused by a lack of calories and protein, resulting in significant loss of muscle mass and subcutaneous fat. It's characterised by emaciation and wasting of the body, often affecting children in developing countries due to factors like poverty and food scarcity.

Vitamins

  • Vitamins are essential, organic substances found in foods that are needed in small amounts for various bodily functions, including growth, metabolism, and nervous system activity.

Types of Vitamins

  1. 1. Water Soluble Vitamins: hese vitamins dissolve in water and are not stored in the body → Vitamin B and Vitamin C.
  2. 2. Fat Soluble Vitamins: These vitamins dissolve in fat and are stored in the body's fatty tissues and liver → Vitamin A, Vitamin D, Vitamin E, Vitamin K.

1912: Casimir Funk, coined the term "Vitamin".

Vitamin D

  • It is also known as "Sunshine Vitamin". It is also considered as a hormone.

Types:

  • Vitamin D2 (Ergocalciferol): Helps in calcium absorption.
  • Vitamin D3 (Cholecalciferol): More effective at raising vitamin D levels in the blood.

Pellagra is also known as 3D Disease.

Sources of Vitamins

Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is a bone disease that develops when bone mineral density and bone mass decreases.

Osteomalacia: Osteomalacia, also known as "soft bones", is a metabolic bone disease that weakens bones and makes them more likely to break.

Minerals

  • Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic chemical elements that the body needs in small amounts for proper development and functioning.
  • Millets like Jowar, Bajra, Ragi have abundant minerals in them.
  • Magnesium: Involved in metabolism, supports bone health. A typical adult human body contains about 25 g of magnesium.
  • Zinc: Important for wound healing, involved in protein synthesis and cell growth.
  • Iodine: Essential component of thyroid hormone which regulates metabolism, growth, and development, iodine also impacts brain function and cognitive development.
  • Excess fluoride in water causes Fluorosis.

Collagen

  • Collagen is the most abundant protein of our body that are found in extracellular spaces (skin, bone joints).
  • Triple helical structure of collagen was discovered by: G. N. Ramachandran.
  • Vitamin C is important for synthesis of collagen.

§ 7NUTRIENTS

§ 8NUTRITION IN PLANTS

Modes of Nutrition

Nutrition diagram:

  • Autotrophic (Green plants, Blue green algae) — Phytoplanktons
  • Heterotrophic (Fungi, Amoeba, Man) → Saprophytic (Fungi, Yeast, Feed on dead and decaying matters) → Parasitic (Cuscuta, Plasmodium, Nematodes) → Holozoic (Man, Dog, Amoeba)
  1. 1. Autotrophic: In this mode of nutrition an organism can produce its own food, using light, water, carbon dioxide, and other chemicals.
  2. 2. Heterotrophic: In this mode of nutrition an organism cannot produce its own food, however, takes nutrition from other organisms, primarily plant or animal matter.

Types:

  • (a) Saprophytic: In this type of nutrition, the organism, particularly fungi, obtain nutrients directly from dead organic matter or wastes.
  • (b) Parasitic: In this type of nutrition, plants derive some or all of its nutrition requirements from another living plant (host).
  • (c) Holozoic: In this type of nutrition, the organism consume solid or liquid food and break it down internally.

Photosynthesis

  • Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water.
  • It takes place in the leaves, in cells containing chlorophyll. Sunlight provides energy to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Carbon dioxide from the air combines with hydrogen to form glucose (sugar). Oxygen is released as a byproduct.

Photosynthesis equation: Carbon dioxide + Water —Sunlight→ Glucose + Oxygen

6CO₂ + 6H₂O —Sunlight→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

  • Chlorophyll makes plant appear green because it absorbs red and blue light from sunlight while reflecting green light.

Light and Dark Reaction in Chloroplast

Chloroplast

  • A chloroplast is an organelle in plant cells and algae that converts sunlight into chemical energy through photosynthesis.

Two types of reactions takes place in Chloroplast:

Light Dependent Reaction

  • The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes where light splits water into Hydrogen and Oxygen in the form of ATP and NADPH.

Light Independent Reaction (Calvin Cycle)

  • The light-independent reactions occur in the stroma where there is a use of ATP and NADPH to convert Carbon Dioxide into Glucose.

Structure of Chloroplast

  • Inner membrane: Controls the movement of materials in and out.
  • Outer membrane: Protective layer; allows small molecules to pass.
  • Stroma: Fluid-filled space where the Calvin cycle occurs.
  • Thylakoids: Disc-shaped sacs that contain chlorophyll.
  • Grana (Granum): Stacks of thylakoids where light reactions take place.
  • Lamella: Membranous bridges connecting grana.

Mesophyll cells are primary site for photosynthesis.

Guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata pores, and they respond to changes in carbon dioxide concentration in leaves.

§ 9NUTRIENTS

  • Legumes such as lentils do not require fertilisers as their roots have Nitrogen Fixing Bacteria such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter. They convert atmospheric Nitrogen into fixed Nitrogen that is usable by plants.

Few Important Terms

  • Xerophytes: Xerophytes are plants adapted to survive in dry or arid environments, characterized by limited water availability.
  • Heliophytes: Heliophytes, also called sun-loving plants, are those that require full exposure to the sun for their optimum growth.
  • Neophytes: A neophyte is a plant species which is not native to a geographical region and was introduced in recent history.
  • Protophytes: Protophyte plants are primitive, simple, and often microscopic plants that represent the earliest forms of plant life.
